papers.title: Dual CD40/CD28 co-stimulation reprograms the solid-tumor microenvironment to unleash CAR-T and endogenous anti-tumor immunity
papers.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has shown limited efficacy against solid tumors, owing to poor T-cell persistence, an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) and cancer immune evasion. Here we describe LACO-Stim (lymphocytes-APC co-stimulator), a chimeric co-stimulatory molecule composed of an agonistic anti-CD40 single-chain variable fragment (scFv) and the CD28 intracellular signaling domain, such that a single molecule activates CD40-expressing antigen-presenting cells while delivering CD28 co-stimulation to the T cell that bears it. Co-expressed with a 4-1BB-based CAR (LACO-CAR-T), it enhanced anti-tumor activity in vitro and achieved durable, complete in most mice, tumor regression rather than transient control in xenograft and immunocompetent models. In immunocompetent hosts, LACO-CAR-T activated dendritic cells, reprogrammed tumor macrophages toward M1-like, antigen-presenting states, and induced epitope spreading with endogenous CD8 T-cell responses against tumor neoantigens. Single-cell transcriptomics and RNA-velocity analysis revealed coordinated immune remodeling: T cells shifted toward a more stem-like, less terminally exhausted state, regulatory T cells declined in frequency and suppressive function, and myeloid cells acquired antigen-presentation programs while excessive inflammatory and suppressive signaling was restrained. LACO-Stim further synergized with anti-PD-1 blockade to control tumor growth. LACO-Stim thus enables CAR-T cells to coordinate intrinsic T-cell reinforcement with extrinsic immune reprogramming, converting an immunosuppressive TME into a de-inflamed (reduced inflammatory signaling), de-suppressed rather than merely armed niche that supports endogenous anti-tumor immunity.

papers.title: IL13 critically contributes to the antitumor activity of polyfunctional CD4+ T cells driven by constitutively active Stat5
papers.abstract: The presence of polyfunctional T cells capable of concurrently producing multiple cytokines correlates with favorable clinical outcomes in patients with cancer. We previously reported that overexpression of constitutively active Stat5a (CASTAT5) confers polyfunctionality on tumor-specific CD4 T cells, enabling durable antitumor immunity following adoptive cell therapy. However, the mechanisms underlying the enhanced antitumor effects of CASTAT5-modified T cells remain unclear. Here, we identify interleukin-13 (IL13) as a critical effector cytokine contributing to the multifaceted antitumor activity of CASTAT5-conditioned polyfunctional CD4 T cells (C5-CD4). C5-CD4 T cells exhibit a prominent T helper 2 (Th2) cytokine profile, accompanied by extensive epigenomic remodeling at the Th2 cytokine loci, as revealed by Hi-C and histone-modification CUT&Tag assays. Neutralization of IL13 diminished the antitumor efficacy of C5-CD4 T cells. Furthermore, targeted Il13 disruption substantially impaired tumor control and was associated with reduced donor T cell expansion and persistence, diminished systemic cytokine and chemokine responses, and attenuated activation of endogenous tumor-reactive CD8 T cells. Nonetheless, IL13 overexpression alone in donor CD4 T cells failed to fully recapitulate the therapeutic activity of C5-CD4 T cells, indicating that IL13 is a critical contributor but is insufficient to account for the full antitumor activity conferred by CASTAT5. Single-cell RNA sequencing associated donor-derived IL13 with increased representation of tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells and IL13-signaling in monocytes and macrophages exhibiting tissue-repair-associated transcriptional programs. Moreover, Il13 disruption diminished the therapeutic efficacy of CASTAT5-expressing CD19-targeted CAR-T cells in a mouse B-cell lymphoma model. Reanalysis of a human CD19CAR-T infusion-product dataset further revealed an association between IL13 expression and type 2 cytokine signatures linked to prolonged clinical response, suggesting a potential contribution of IL13 to the efficacy of human CD19CAR-T therapy. Together, these findings uncover an unexpected antitumor role for IL13 and establish it as a critical node linking polyfunctional donor T cells with endogenous immune cells to promote sustained tumor immunity.

papers.title: Identification and localization of bone marrow ILC2s using Id2/Cxcr6 dual-reporter mice
papers.abstract: Type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) are present in the bone marrow, where their identification and spatial localization remain challenging because of their low abundance and the expression of shared markers by other lymphoid populations. Here, we evaluated the use of Id2YFP/+ Cxcr6GFP/+ dual-reporter mice to identify and visualize bone marrow ILC2s. Using spectral flow cytometry, we showed that both ST2- and ST2 ILC2s expressed high levels of ID2, whereas CXCR6 expression differed between these subsets. However, the ID2 expressing compartments also contained NK cells, NKT cells, conventional T cells and ILC progenitors. Surface marker profiling identified CD25 and ICOS as useful markers for enriching ILC2 populations, with ST2 enabling the segregation of the ST2- and ST2 subsets. Single-cell RNA sequencing further characterized the diversity of Id2 and Cxcr6 expressing lymphoid populations and supported the use of CD5 and NKp46 as exclusion markers. Combining these markers with the dual-reporter system, confocal microscopy revealed YFPGFPCD5-NKp46- cells compatible with an ILC2 phenotype, distributed throughout the bone marrow as isolated cells or within multicellular clusters. Complementary flow cytometric analyses demonstrated that ILC2s accounted for more than 90% of a phenotypically related reporter-positive population after exclusion of major T and NK cell populations, providing additional support for the identification of the cells visualized in situ as putative ILC2s. Together, these findings establish a strategy combining dual-reporter mice, flow cytometry, transcriptomic profiling and confocal imaging to investigate the localization and spatial organization of putative bone marrow ILC2s.

papers.title: Deep CyTOF immune profiles of ex vivo granulomatous responses to Mycobacterium tuberculosis differ with European and African geographical origin
papers.abstract: Genetic and environmental factors influence human immunity and modulate responses to infection. Accounting for immune heterogeneity across human populations is critical to the design of novel vaccines and host-directed interventions that would optimally benefit populations experiencing the highest disease burden. Tuberculosis (TB) burden is unevenly distributed across geographical regions and our understanding of the differential immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) across human populations remains limited. Here, we sought to evaluate the impact of geographical origin on ex vivo granulomatous responses to Mtbinfection. We found that peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from healthy African donors exhibited greater control of Mtbgrowth ex vivo than those isolated from European individuals. High-dimensional single-cell profiling of the granulomatous responses by cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) revealed divergent profiles based on the specimens' geographical origin. Monocytes from European donors displayed a pro-inflammatory phenotype - correlating with Mtbgrowth -, whereas PBMCs of African individuals were enriched in activated, cytotoxic T cells - correlating with Mtbcontrol. Reduced inflammatory response in African monocytes following various microbial stimulations was confirmed. Taken together, our comprehensive immune profiling indicates that environmental and genetic factors shape a cytotoxic-regulatory response that promotes bacterial control. Against the current "one-treatment-fits-all" approach, our findings support the use of specimens from intervention-relevant settings to inform the targeted design of TB vaccines and host-directed interventions.

papers.title: Systemic TLR7 agonism moderates disease severity in acute DSS-induced colitis in mice
papers.abstract: Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) is an endosomal sensor of single-stranded RNA, studied for its antiviral and pro-inflammatory functions. Its role in intestinal inflammation is undefined, and no approved or clinical-stage therapy for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) engages this pathway. Here we report that systemic administration of the reference TLR7 agonist GS-9620 (vesatolimod) moderates disease severity in acute dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced colitis in mice. GS-9620-treated mice lost less weight, had lower Disease Activity Index scores, and were protected from DSS-induced colon shortening. Immunophenotyping of the spleen showed reduced Th17 and Tr17 populations and an increased proportion of regulatory T cells. These findings indicate that pharmacological TLR7 agonism is not merely tolerated in the inflamed intestine but is associated with a shift of the systemic immune compartment toward a regulatory phenotype. The results identify TLR7 as a candidate disease-moderating target in IBD and motivate direct tests of causality, route and chronic-disease relevance.

papers.title: Deep phenomics of African green monkey and Baboon PBMCs using a 30-marker spectral flow cytometry panel
papers.abstract: Vaccines are the best way to prevent and combat diseases. Non-human primate (NHP) models have proven to be the gold standard model for studying the efficacy of certain vaccine candidates prior to human trials. Cell-mediated immunity serves as a surrogate marker for predicting vaccine efficacy. Despite the availability of deep-immunophenotyping panels for T cells in the peripheral blood of humans, their application to NHPs, particularly African Green Monkeys (AGMs) and baboons, remains limited. Notably, AGMs are valuable for HIV and COVID-19 research, while baboons are utilized for pertussis research as a natural infection model and vaccine trial. To overcome such limitation, using spectral flow cytometry, we developed a 30-parameter panel to profile major immune cell subsets (B cells, NK cells, DCs, monocytes) either in AGM or baboon PBMCs. We also profiled T cells, memory phenotypes, functional cytokines by tracking established Th1 markers IFN{gamma}, TNF and IL-2; Th2 markers IL-4/5/13 and the Th17 marker, IL-17, activation-induced markers (AIMs) and FoxP3+ Tregs in both AGM and baboon PBMCs in steady state as well as in mitogen stimulated conditions. For AIMs, CD69, CD134 (OX40) and CD137 (4-1BB) are included and validated in both NHP species. This panel holds potential for exploratory analysis of the impact of these functional cytokines, AIMs, or Tregs on host immunity following infection or vaccination. The panels high level of customization empowers researchers to tailor it to their specific research needs.

papers.title: Cholinergic modulation engages a CHRM1-IL-17 neuroimmune axis to promote diabetic wound repair
papers.abstract: Chronic non-healing wounds are a major complication of diabetes, where persistent inflammation fails to transition into effective tissue repair (1-3). Here we identify cholinergic modulation as a mechanism that promotes productive inflammation and diabetic wound healing. Using a healing-associated fibroblast signature derived from single-cell profiling of human diabetic foot ulcers (3), we identified the acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitor metrifonate as a candidate inducer of reparative wound programs. Topical delivery accelerated healing in diabetic mice and increased acetylcholine availability within the wound. Complementary receptor pharmacology identified muscarinic acetylcholine receptor 1 (CHRM1) as the principal receptor mediating the reparative response. Transcriptomic and cellular analyses revealed early induction of IL-17-associated inflammatory programs and enrichment of CHRM1NK1.1 innate lymphocytes. Depletion of NK1.1 cells or neutralization of IL-17A abolished the pro-healing effect, whereas spatial transcriptomics revealed treatment-associated organization of NK cells within vascular niches. Localized treatment further promoted repair in diabetic porcine wounds and human skin models. Together, these findings identify a CHRM1-IL-17 neuroimmune axis linking cholinergic modulation to diabetic wound repair and establish local AChE inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy for chronic wounds.

papers.title: Impaired Fermentation in the Absence of Gut Microbiota Promotes Inulin-Induced Intestinal Inflammation
papers.abstract: Background and aims: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are characterized by altered gut microbiota composition and impaired dietary fiber fermentation, which can complicate symptom management. Although inulin is a well-established prebiotic fiber, it can exacerbate gut inflammation under certain conditions. We hypothesized that impaired microbial fermentation leaves intact inulin in the gut to activate epithelial immune receptors and promote inflammation, whereas effective fermentation reduces this pro-inflammatory signaling. Methods: We used germ-free (GF) and conventional (CONV) interleukin-10 knockout (Il10-/-) and wild-type (WT) C57BL/6J mice to assess the role of microbial fermentation and host genetic susceptibility in IBD. GF Il10-/- mice were colonized with fecal microbiota from ulcerative colitis (UC) patients or healthy individuals with fiber intolerance (FI). Mice were fed inulin or structurally distinct, physicochemically matched fiber analogs. Colonic inflammatory and barrier-related gene expression and protein levels were assessed by qPCR and ELISA. Results: In GF Il10-/- mice, inulin, but not cellulose, induced weight loss, diarrhea, and rectal prolapse. Increased colonic toll-like receptor expression (TLR2, TLR4) as well as elevated serum amyloid A (SAA) and lipocalin-2 levels indicated immune activation by unfermented inulin in GF mice. Colonization with dysbiotic microbiota attenuated these effects. {beta}-fructan fibers including fructooligosaccharides and chicory-derived inulin elicited marked inflammatory responses, whereas agave-derived inulin did not, highlighting the influence of fiber composition in inflammation associated with IBD. Conclusions: Effective microbial fermentation is essential for host tolerance to fermentable fibers. These findings underscore the need of personalized nutrition when recommending fiber supplementation in immune-compromised individuals or those with gut dysbiosis.

papers.title: The Src family kinases Lck and Fyn promote transendothelial migration of T cells
papers.abstract: The ability of T cells to cross endothelial barriers and migrate into and within peripheral tissue is crucial for adaptive immunity. Integrins such as LFA-1 play an essential role in this process by acting as adhesion molecules and initiating signaling events that drive the cytoskeletal changes needed for cell migration, however, many of the specific signaling events that promote T cell migration are still unknown. Here, we found that the Src family kinases Lck and Fyn are needed for efficient T cell migration. Primary T cells lacking Lck, Fyn, or both kinases exhibited defects in random migration on ICAM-1 coated surfaces for parameters such as speed and mean squared displacement. Analysis of signaling revealed that Lck was required for PI3K signaling downstream of LFA-1, while Fyn was not. Mechanistically, we found that the absence of Lck disrupted the normal interaction of the PI3K regulatory subunit p85 with tyrosine-phosphorylated binding partners, suggesting that Lck may regulate PI3K activity by controlling p85 protein-protein interactions. Importantly, both Lck and Fyn were required for efficient T cell transmigration across an inflamed endothelial barrier, a critical event for tissue infiltration. Lastly, a small-molecule Lck kinase inhibitor also decreased PI3K signaling and T cell transmigration, indicating the kinase activity of Lck is needed. Together, these data identify a new role for Lck and Fyn in promoting T cell transmigration.

papers.title: IL4Ra Controls The Medullary Dwell Time Of Mature Thymocytes By Scheduling Their Release From The Thymus
papers.abstract: Following their generation, newly produced single positive (SP) thymocytes must remain in the thymus to undergo post-selection maturation, a process supported by the thymic medulla. This ensures that SP thymocytes are equipped with functional competence prior to S1PR1-mediated thymic emigration. Despite this importance, the intrathymic mechanisms that control the balance between retention and release of SP thymocytes is unclear. Here, we describe a cell autonomous requirement for IL4Ra-signalling in SP thymocytes, that determines the duration of their medullary occupancy. We show that the period of this occupancy is prolonged in the absence of IL4R expression by SP thymocytes, which occurs as a result of impaired interactions with medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTEC). Importantly, extending the duration of medullary occupancy enhances the maturational status and functional capabilities of SP thymocytes, including improved TNF and IL2 production. Collectively, we show that IL4Ra regulates the medullary occupancy of mature thymocytes, which in turn determines the functional properties of thymic output.

papers.title: TMEM11-Dependent Cristae Architecture Restrains Imiquimod-Induced NLRP3 Inflammasome Activation via Mitochondrial ROS
papers.abstract: Imiquimod (IMQ) is a clinically approved drug widely used to treat skin malignancies; however, its application frequently provokes severe inflammation through NLRP3 inflammasome activation. The mechanism underlying IMQ-induced activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome is not completely defined. While IMQ-induced inhibition of mitochondrial electron transport chain complex I is necessary for activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, it is not sufficient; suggesting presence of additional targets/triggers. The role of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) as the additional trigger to activate the inflammasome remains contentious based on conflicting reports. Using a unique genetic model lacking expression of mitochondrial membrane protein TMEM11 we reaffirm the role of mtROS in IMQ-induced NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Macrophages deficient in Tmem11, a mitochondrial contact site and cristae organizing system (MICOS)-associated membrane-protein, exhibit ultrastructural defects in cristae morphology without altering mitochondrial mass or mtDNA copy number. Loss of TMEM11 influences cristae length and density, reducing mitochondrial oxygen consumption. Tmem11-deficient macrophages exhibit normal NLRP3 inflammasome activation in response to canonical agonists (e.g., ATP, nigericin) but show caspase-1 hyperactivation and exaggerated IL-1{beta} and IL-18 secretion upon IMQ treatment. This exaggerated response is rescued by antioxidant treatment, confirming the role for mtROS. These findings demonstrate that cristae architecture restrains drug-induced mtROS to limit NLRP3 activation and that mtROS is a primary driver of IMQ-mediated NLRP3 inflammasome activation.

papers.title: Structural evolution of Fcα/μR-mediated antibody recognition
papers.abstract: The Fc alpha-mu receptor (Fc/R) is an ancient Fc-receptor sharing common ancestry with the polymeric Ig receptor (pIgR) and binding polymeric IgM and IgA ligands. In several vertebrate lineages, including birds, Fc/R may serve as the sole IgM and IgA Fc receptor; yet its evolution and ligand-recognition mechanisms across vertebrates remain poorly understood. Here, we identify FCAMR expression in duck (Anas platyrhynchos, ap) lymphoid tissues and demonstrate that recombinantly expressed apFc/R ectodomain binds apIgM and apIgA ligands. apFc/R affinity was ~10-fold higher for apIgM versus apIgA and ~10-fold higher than mouse (mm) Fc/R. Cryo-EM structures of apFc/R in complex with pentameric apIgM (3.27 [A]) and tetrameric apIgA (3.57 [A]) showed three Ig-like domains (D1-D3) bound asymmetrically with 1:1 stoichiometry. Comparisons to avian pIgR, which contains four Ig-like domains (D1-D4), revealed overlapping contacts between apFc/R-D1 and pIgR-D1. apFc/R D2-D3 engaged sites similar to pIgR D3-D4, yet formed distinct contact networks. Parallel analysis of a mmFc/R-mmIgM structure (4.13 [A]) revealed mmFc/R's single Ig-domain bound analogous to apFc/R-D1 and to mammalian pIgR-D1, whereas downstream ectodomain regions were not observed. Collectively, the data elucidate PIGR-family mechanisms across vertebrates, providing a foundation for delineating common and divergent functions.

papers.title: Circulating CD4 regulatory T cells are broadly preserved in Parkinson's disease despite altered HELIOS expression
papers.abstract: Background Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are an important component of adaptive immune regulation and have been implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), with previous studies suggesting altered Treg proportions, phenotype and, in some cases, function. However, existing studies have been limited by variable phenotyping approaches and a lack of detailed functional assessment. Given the growing interest in Tregs as potential therapies in PD, better understanding of their phenotype and function in the disease is important. Methods Circulating FOXP3+ Tregs were characterised in individuals with PD and age-matched healthy controls (HC) using a 24-colour spectral flow cytometry panel. Treg suppressive function was assessed by their ability to inhibit proliferation and cytokine production by polyclonally stimulated autologous T effector cells in vitro. Treg lineage stability was assessed by analysis of FOXP3 TSDR demethylation. Results The proportions and phenotypic characteristics of circulating CD4 Tregs were broadly similar between individuals with PD and HCs, as were Treg suppressive function and FOXP3 TSDR demethylation. However, naive CD4 Tregs from individuals with PD showed reduced HELIOS expression, with a similar but non-significant trend in FOXP3 expression. Reduced HELIOS expression was also observed in the CD8 naive Treg compartment. Conclusions Major quantitative or functional abnormalities in circulating Tregs do not appear to be a dominant feature PD. However, reduced HELIOS expression in naive Tregs suggests more subtle phenotypic alterations that warrant further investigation. The broadly preserved suppressive function is reassuring for therapeutic approaches aimed at increasing Treg numbers, although it will be important to establish that expanded Tregs retain a stable phenotype and suppressive function in inflammatory and tissue environments.

papers.title: Photomechanical engineering of immunogenic whole-cell vaccines by laser-induced vapor nanobubbles for bladder cancer prophylaxis
papers.abstract: Whole-cell cancer vaccines can provide broad tumor-antigen repertoires, but their efficacy depends on manufacturing methods that inactivate tumor cells while preserving immunogenic danger signals. Here we show that laser-induced vapor nanobubbles (VNB) generated from dextran-coated iron oxide nanoparticles provide a drug-free photomechanical route to engineer immunogenic whole-cell vaccines against bladder cancer. Using MB49 murine urothelial carcinoma cells, we established VNB conditions that induced rapid tumor-cell killing together with calreticulin exposure and extracellular ATP and HMGB1 release. Rapid cell killing and calreticulin exposure were also reproduced in the molecularly distinct UPPL1541 bladder cancer model, supporting the generalizability of the early photomechanical response across bladder cancer cell lines. Vaccination with VNB-killed MB49 cells reduced tumor incidence and growth after subcutaneous challenge and enhanced splenocyte-mediated antitumor activity against MB49 cells. In an orthotopic bladder cancer model, vaccination prevented MRI-detectable tumor formation and was associated with marked early bladder enrichment of CD8 T cells and inflammatory monocytes. A single administration of the VNB-generated vaccine preparation showed no evident local or systemic toxicity during seven days of follow-up. These findings provide proof of concept for an externally triggered, drug-free manufacturing approach in which short laser irradiation induces rapid photomechanical killing of tumor cells on demand, generating immunogenic whole-tumor-cell vaccine preparations for further evaluation in therapeutic, post-resection and tumor-derived settings.

papers.title: ATF3 Preserves Macrophage Cholesterol Homeostasis during Metabolic Stress
papers.abstract: Background: Macrophages must coordinate immune activation with maintenance of cellular cholesterol homeostasis, yet the transcriptional mechanisms integrating these processes remain incompletely understood. Activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3) suppresses inflammatory and interferon responses and has been implicated in macrophage lipid metabolism, suggesting a role in coordinating immune and sterol-responsive transcriptional programs. Methods: Wild-type and ATF3-deficient bone marrow-derived macrophages were analyzed by bulk RNA sequencing following Toll-like receptor stimulation and under conditions of sterol loading or depletion. Cholesterol content, cytokine production, and sterol-responsive gene expression were quantified. Human metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) datasets and Kupffer cell-specific ATF3 knockout mice were used to assess disease relevance in vivo. Results: ATF3 deficiency enhanced inflammatory and interferon-responsive transcriptional programs while suppressing a sterol-responsive gene module enriched for SREBP2 target genes. This phenotype was conserved across diverse Toll-like receptor stimuli and accompanied by persistent Ch25h upregulation. Despite exhibiting elevated cellular cholesterol, ATF3-deficient macrophages retained transcriptional responsiveness to sterol loading and depletion while demonstrating reduced induction of SREBP2-dependent genes across conditions. IFNAR blockade reduced interferon-responsive gene expression but did not normalize Ch25h or sterol-responsive gene expression. In contrast, CRISPR-mediated reduction of Ch25h partially restored sterol-responsive gene expression in inflammatory ATF3-deficient macrophages. In human MASLD, hepatic ATF3 expression positively correlated with disease severity. In mice, ATF3 was preferentially induced in Kupffer cells during metabolic stress, and Kupffer cell-specific deletion of ATF3 increased liver injury and Kupffer cell lipid accumulation. Conclusions: ATF3 supports sterol-responsive transcriptional programs while restraining inflammatory activation in macrophages. ATF3 loss results in elevated cellular cholesterol, impaired SREBP2-dependent gene expression, and persistent derepression of Ch25h, which contributes to but does not fully explain the sterol phenotype. These findings identify ATF3 as a coordinator of macrophage adaptation to inflammatory and metabolic stress and support a protective role for Kupffer cell ATF3 during metabolic liver disease.

papers.title: Therapeutic anti-IgE antibodies generate distinct functional immune complex signatures
papers.abstract: Therapeutic IgG anti-IgE antibodies are benchmarked by their ability to interfere with IgE-Fc[epsilon]RI binding, but their activity within IgE and IgG-containing immune complexes remains poorly defined. Here we show that omalizumab and ligelizumab form binary IgE-IgG and ternary allergen-containing immune complexes with distinct functional properties. In primary human leukocytes, these complexes exhibited antibody- and composition-dependent patterns of cellular association and activation. Using multiplexed focal molography, we resolved Fc receptor engagement across free and complexed antibody states and identified distinct receptor-binding signatures for omalizumab- and ligelizumab-containing complexes. Notably, allergen incorporation reversed the relative ability of the two antibodies to neutralize IgE-Fc[epsilon]RI interactions and remodelled Fc[gamma]R binding. Thus, immune-complex composition is a determinant of therapeutic antibody function.

papers.title: Proliferation and mutation as humoral immune response
papers.abstract: The affinity maturation process, through which antibodies acquire relatively high affinity for an invading pathogen, involves complex mechanisms whose relative importance is not yet fully understood. This study proposes an analytical model of this process, to investigate the main factors governing proliferation and mutation and assess their respective roles. The model suggests that the immune system should not be expected to follow a single, rigid evolutionary pattern, as a wide range of proliferation and mutation strategies can yield nearly optimal outcomes. Keywords: Antibody, antigen, affinity, B-cell, mutation, proliferation

papers.title: Proteome-wide discovery of novel diagnostic antigens for coccidioidomycosis
papers.abstract: Coccidioidomycosis, commonly called Valley Fever (VF), caused by Coccidioides spp., is an understudied fungal disease that accounts for a substantial fraction of pneumonias in endemic areas. Diagnosis remains challenging because the mainstay of diagnosis is serology, and current assays have modest sensitivity in early infection. Discovery of new antigens could improve serologic detection early in disease. Here, we use PepSeq, a DNA-programmable serology platform, to represent the complete proteome of Coccidioides within a library of 244,000 DNA-barcoded peptides. By profiling antibody reactivity at the protein and epitope levels in VF patients, naturally infected pigtail macaques, and healthy controls, we identify numerous previously-unrecognized antigens and epitopes, including some shared between humans and macaque responses. When translated into a pooled peptide ELISA, we show that a subset of identified antigens can discriminate VF cases from controls in an independent cohort with high accuracy (AUC = 0.91). These findings establish high-dimensional peptide serology as a scalable approach for fungal antigen discovery and identify new targets for improved VF diagnosis.

papers.title: Microglial AhR Drives Sex-Biased Amyloid Pathology
papers.abstract: Microglia integrate local and systemic signals that can modify their response to amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}), but the molecular pathways connecting these signals to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), a sensor of microbiota- and host-derived metabolites, as a microglial regulator of amyloid pathology. Sustained administration of the AhR agonist indoxyl-3-sulfate (I3S) exacerbated cortical A{beta} deposition and plaque-associated neuritic damage in APPNL-F mice. Conversely, constitutive AhR deficiency reduced amyloid burden, promoted plaque compaction, and preserved behavioural performance, whereas inducible deletion of AhR in microglia was sufficient to reduce plaque accumulation. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that AhR loss reprogrammed microglia toward phagolysosomal and A{beta}-recognition states and enhanced microglial A{beta} uptake, with markedly stronger effects in females. APPNL-F mice also exhibited sex-dependent remodelling of the gut microbiota and tryptophan-derived metabolites. Circulating indole-3-aldehyde (IAld) robustly activated AhR and was associated with cortical amyloid pathology. AhR-activating bioactivity was increased in mouse serum, cortex and faecal extracts and was higher in serum from the COGNIBIO12 analytical subcohort than in independently recruited cognitively unimpaired H2H participants. Among amyloid-positive patients, higher serum AhR bioactivity was associated with lower CSF A{beta}42 concentrations. Together, these findings identify microglial AhR as a metabolically responsive regulator linking systemic ligand availability, biological sex, and microglial control of amyloid pathology.

papers.title: Onsite fixation preserves phosphoprotein profile in human whole blood
papers.abstract: Phospho-flow cytometry is increasingly used as a pharmacodynamic readout of kinase-pathway activity, including in JAK inhibitor trials. Phosphoprotein states are intrinsically labile ex vivo and are further altered by conventional workflows, which typically involve PBMC isolation, cryopreservation, and transit times of hours to days before measurement. Here, we fix whole blood at collection and quantify six phosphoproteins by mass cytometry, benchmarked against matched cryopreserved PBMCs. Unlike PBMCs, whole blood retained neutrophils, ~75-80% of which were pSTAT3-positive at baseline. Basal pSTAT3 was also markedly higher in whole blood monocytes (~41% positive vs. ~9% in PBMCs), whereas T, B, and NK cells differed by less than 1 percentage point. Stimulation produced subset-specific phosphorylation patterns that were retained after 6 weeks of storage. Because fixation does not require centrifugation and retains neutrophils, samples can be fixed at collection sites without on-site processing laboratories and analyzed centrally in batches.

papers.title: Establishing an ex vivo platform for molecular profiling of skin structural cells using frozen human skin biopsies
papers.abstract: Skin structural cells, including keratinocytes, melanocytes, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts, play critical roles in the development of chronic inflammatory skin disease. Inflammatory stimuli induce transcriptional reprogramming and epigenetic changes in skin structural cells, which contribute to disease pathogenesis. Although two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) skin culture models have been widely used to investigate inflammatory responses in skin structural cells, ex vivo systems that maintain skin structure and cellular composition remain limited. To address this gap, we explored using frozen skin biopsies as an experimental platform to study the responses of skin structural cells to inflammatory stimuli. Using a simple air-liquid interface culture method on permeable Transwell inserts, we showed that viable skin structural cells that retain cell-type-specific transcriptional profiles can be recovered from frozen skin biopsies after prolonged in vitro culture. Stimulation with IFN-{gamma} induced robust transcriptional and chromatin accessibility changes that were largely resolved after stimulus removal, with transcriptional responses to secondary stimulation comparable to the primary stimulation. Treatment of cultured skin biopsies with histone-modifying enzyme inhibitors effectively altered global histone modification levels, but did not substantially affect the transcriptional resolution of IFN-{gamma}-induced responses. Collectively, these findings establish cryopreserved human skin biopsies as a scalable ex vivo platform that enables mechanistic studies of inflammatory responses of multiple populations of skin structural cells.

papers.title: Galectin-9 drives thrombo-inflammatory circuits initiating venous thrombosis
papers.abstract: Background: Venous thromboembolism is increasingly recognized as a thrombo-inflammatory disease, yet the pathways linking inflammation to venous thrombus initiation remain incompletely defined. Galectin-9 (Gal-9), a {beta}-galactoside-binding lectin elevated in inflammatory disorders, has no defined role in venous thrombosis. Methods: Using plasma from patients with deep vein thrombosis (DVT), Gal-9-deficient mice, an inferior vena cava stenosis model, intravital microscopy, microfluidics, and ex vivo platelet and neutrophil assays, we assessed the functional contribution of Gal-9 to venous thrombosis. Results: Plasma Gal-9 was elevated in DVT patients, correlated with D-dimer at presentation, and declined over 3-month follow-up. Gal-9 deletion did not alter hemostasis but markedly impaired thrombus initiation, with reduced platelet and neutrophil recruitment to the vessel wall and reduced intra-thrombus neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. TNF-/IFN-{gamma}-stimulated endothelial cells upregulated Gal-9 and promoted platelet adhesion and fibrin(ogen) deposition, which Gal-9 neutralization partially reversed. Under venous shear, immobilized recombinant Gal-9 potentiated platelet activation and thrombus formation, particularly alongside collagen, whereas Gal-9 inhibition suppressed these responses. Gal-9-activated platelets promoted NETosis and shifted thrombus composition toward a NET-rich inflammatory phenotype. Conclusions: Gal-9 is a previously unrecognized driver of venous thrombo-inflammation, linking vascular inflammation to platelet activation, NET formation, and thrombosis. Genetic deletion attenuated these responses in vivo, and antibody-mediated Gal-9 neutralization suppressed platelet activation and thrombus formation in vitro, identifying the Gal-9 glycan-binding pathway as a therapeutic target that disrupts thrombosis without impairing hemostasis.

papers.title: A novel KIR3DL2-directed CAR T-cell therapy for cutaneous and systemic T-cell lymphomas
papers.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of B-cell malignancies and multiple myeloma, but its extension to T-cell lymphomas (TCLs) has been constrained by the paucity of antigens that can be safely targeted. While targeting pan-T antigens broadens the therapeutic reach across various TCLs, it carries a substantial risk of immunosuppression and infection. Here, we report killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor, three Ig domains and long cytoplasmic tail 2 (KIR3DL2/CD158k) as a viable target for CAR T-cell therapy against a wide range of TCLs. Using single-cell RNA-seq data analysis and flow cytometric phenotyping, we observed that KIR3DL2 expression is restricted to a subset of mature NK cells and a minor fraction of CD8 T cells, with negligible expression in other healthy adult tissues. Among TCLs, KIR3DL2 expression was noted in various subtypes of cutaneous and systemic TCLs. Anti-KIR3DL2 CAR constructs (3DL2CARs) efficiently and selectively redirected T cells against antigen-positive cell lines but not isogenic KIR3DL2-negative counterparts, with antigen-specific signaling, cytotoxicity, proliferation, and cytokine production. Importantly, 3DL2CART cells produced sustained tumor regression and prolonged survival in two distinct cell line-derived xenograft models of cutaneous TCL and in one patient-derived xenograft model of hepatosplenic TCL. 3DL2CART cells exhibited minimal off-target activity against bystander immune cells and showed no appreciable fratricide. To mitigate the risk of tumor cell contamination in autologous CAR T-cell products, we established a two-tiered strategy that integrates immunomagnetic depletion of KIR3DL2-positive tumor cells with in vivo activation of a safety switch if inadvertently transduced malignant cells contribute to immune escape. Together, our results establish the preclinical efficacy and safety of 3DL2CART-cell therapy and support its clinical translation. This approach may offer a targeted alternative to pan-T-cell-directed CAR T-cell strategies for patients with relapsed/refractory cutaneous and systemic TCLs, addressing a critical unmet clinical need.

papers.title: Hypoxia-inducible factor 2-alpha promotes fitness of cytokine-activated human natural killer cells
papers.abstract: Natural Killer (NK) cells are innate effector cells with potent antiviral, antitumor, and immunoregulatory functions that are relevant for the treatment of human diseases. There is a pressing need to better understand the mechanisms governing cellular fitness and functional persistence of NK cells to generate therapeutics regimens of sufficient durability to achieve meaningful clinical benefit. Given the central role of interleukin-2 (IL-2) and IL-15 in the survival and proliferation of NK cells, we sought to identify transcription factors induced by these cytokines that are essential for maintaining the fitness of human NK cells from healthy human blood donors. Culture in IL-2 or IL-15 increased protein expression of hypoxia inducible factor 2 alpha (HIF-2, encoded by EPAS1) but not HIF-1 in NK cells. Unexpectedly, induction of HIF-2 was not dependent on limited oxygen availability. CRISPR targeting of EPAS1 or pharmacological inhibition of HIF-2 protein expression markedly compromised the survival of cytokine-activated human NK cells. In contrast, inhibition of canonical HIF-2 transcription factor activity via blocking HIF-2/HIF-1{beta} heterodimer formation had no apparent effects on NK cell viability, function, or metabolism. These results suggest that cytokines, rather than hypoxia, activate an unconventional HIF-1{beta} independent, HIF-2 pathway that helps to maintain NK cells during cellular activation, revealing the potential promise of manipulating HIF-2 to improve the efficacy of adoptive NK cell therapies.

papers.title: Homeostatic fibroblast niche collapse in clinically uninvolved skin marks a pre-fibrotic stage of systemic sclerosis
papers.abstract: Systemic sclerosis, or scleroderma, is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by vasculopathy, immune dysregulation, and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs. Heterogeneous clinical presentation and polygenic risk complicate our understanding of disease mechanisms and the path to effective therapy. Single-cell analyses have revealed substantial transcriptional diversity in skin, but disease-associated reprogramming remains poorly defined. To address this, we performed high-resolution spatial transcriptomic profiling of paired clinically uninvolved and clinically affected scleroderma donor skin alongside healthy controls. We identified a continuum of cellular, molecular, and spatial changes to the stroma that were already evident in clinically uninvolved tissue yet remained distinct from the broader and more advanced changes in paired fibrotic biopsies. Uninvolved skin was comparable to healthy tissue by clinical and histopathological assessment, but distinguishable by the numerical reduction, transcriptional reprogramming, and spatial isolation of LGR5+SCARA5+PI16+ progenitor fibroblasts. In parallel, the dermal vascular smooth muscle compartment shifted from a contractile to a synthetic, activated state, suggesting reprogramming that begins before overt fibrosis. Cell neighborhood analysis revealed that progenitor fibroblasts occupy dense stromal niches in healthy skin that collapse in clinically uninvolved tissue, replaced by isolated, disease-associated fibroblast populations. These data indicate that clinically uninvolved skin occupies an intermediate stage along the pathologic continuum of scleroderma, establishing a framework for strategies to allow early diagnosis and preserve homeostatic fibroblast niches before irreversible tissue remodeling and fibrotic commitment.

papers.title: Preferential Isoform Usage and Isoform Switching in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Patients with Distinct Autoantibody Profile
papers.abstract: RNA sequencing has advanced our understanding of molecular heterogeneity in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), yet most studies have focused on differential gene expression (DGE), which overlooks transcript-level complexity. Alternative splicing and polyadenylation generate multiple isoforms from a single gene, and their dysregulation may contribute to autoimmune pathogenesis, including through the production of non-canonical isoforms with potential autoantigenic properties. To explore this underexamined dimension, we analysed differential isoform usage (DIU) and major isoform switching (MIS) across SLE subgroups stratified by autoantibody profile: anti-dsDNA+, anti-ENA+ and anti-dsDNA+ENA+. Subgroup-specific DIU and MIS events were enriched in RNA-binding and transcription-related functions. In the anti-dsDNA+ subgroup, the T-cell receptor adaptor GRAP2 showed isoform switching accompanied by expansion of a non-coding retained-intron transcript. In the anti-ENA+ subgroup, IGHM switched from the membrane-bound to the secretory form, consistent with an antibody-secreting cell signature; NACA, a reported IgE autoantigen, showed isoform switching; and BRI3, linked to TNF--induced cell death, switched toward its protein-coding transcript. In the anti-dsDNA+ENA+ subgroup, TNFAIP2, a TNF--induced gene, showed isoform redistribution with loss of a uORF-containing transcript. These findings highlight isoform regulation as a distinct, subgroup-specific and functionally relevant layer of transcriptomic dysregulation in SLE.

papers.title: TACO: An open, interpretable model for microsecond-scale TCR specificity prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting antigen-induced T-cell activation from T-cell receptor (TCR) and peptide sequence remains difficult for TCRs and peptides not represented in training data. We present TACO (T-Cell Activation from Chemistry and Orientation), an open statistical model for predicting TCR specificity against HLA-A*02:01-presented peptides. TACO takes as input the peptide sequence and six TCR CDR loop sequences. Learning from binary activation labels, TACO selects a single canonical orientation of the CDR loops over the peptide and learns five amino-acid contact-potential matrices as well as two peptide-exposure profiles.The orientation is fixed and does not require experimentally determined or predicted structures. We evaluate TACO on held-out peptides separated by Levenshtein distance at least four from all training and validation peptides, limiting near-neighbor shortcut learning. TACO achieves AUROC 0.67 on a large held-out activation dataset and 0.68 on IMMREP25 HLA-A*02:01, exceeding the open structure-based models evaluated here and matching the reported AlphaFold3-TCRdock result. The model has 2,019 fitted parameters, retains most within-peptide ranking signal with TCR$beta$ sequence alone, and reaches 406,000 TCR--peptide predictions per second on CPU. This throughput enables computational evaluation of large TCR-peptide search spaces. We show its potential use for prioritizing candidate target peptides from large peptide libraries, reducing the search space for downstream experimental investigation. TACO fitted parameters also expose candidate physicochemical patterns that can be inspected directly. We release TACO's parameters and complete training, evaluation, and inference code.

papers.title: TGF-b/TIF1g signaling restrains CD8+ T cell expansion while preserving cytotoxic competence
papers.abstract: Transforming growth factor b exerts complex and often opposing effects on CD8+ T cell biology, yet the molecular mechanisms that distinguish these functions remain poorly understood. Here, we identify TIF1g (TRIM33) as a critical signal threshold regulator that couples TGF b signaling to CD8+ T cell activation and cytotoxic function. In the presence of TGF b, TIF1g deficient CD8+ T cells bypass canonical suppressive signals and acquire a transcriptional program characterized by enhanced activation and proliferation. Despite this hyperactivated state, TIF1g deficient cells fail to acquire full effector function, exhibiting markedly reduced Granzyme B and Perforin expression under TGF b signaling. We confirmed this functional uncoupling in vivo using a secondary Listeria monocytogenes challenge model, in which TIF1g deficient CD8+ T cells underwent robust expansion yet failed to efficiently control bacterial infection because of impaired cytotoxic activity. In a lymphopenic homeostatic proliferation model, TIF1g deficiency disrupted cellular quiescence, leading to excessive proliferation and spontaneous effector differentiation. Consistent with these findings, loss of TIF1g accelerated B16 melanoma growth and was associated with reduced Perforin expression in tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells. Together, these findings identify TIF1g as a key regulator of TGF b mediated CD8+ T cell responses, uncoupling activation from cytotoxic differentiation and revealing a mechanism by which TGF b independently regulates proliferative and effector programs.

papers.title: Monounsaturated fatty acid depletion is a metabolic pattern of pathogenesis surveilled to activate p38 MAPK innate immunity
papers.abstract: Pathogen infection profoundly remodels host metabolism. Whether hosts sense specific pathogen-induced metabolic changes to identify microbial infection is not known. Here, we find that depletion the monounsaturated fatty acid oleate is a metabolic pattern of pathogenesis, specifically surveilled by the nematode C. elegans to identify active infection with a bacterial pathogen. We previously demonstrated that the enzymatic TIR (Toll/interleukin-1 receptor/resistance)-domain containing protein, TIR-1/SARM1, the key upstream activator of p38 MAPK PMK-1 immunity, is a guard protein in an effector-triggered immune response, positioned specifically on the surface of lysosome-related organelles to sense the toxic effects of bacterial infection. Here, we show that acute loss of oleate in intestinal cells during bacterial infection causes lysosome-related organelles to collapse, which induces the aggregation and activation of TIR-1/SARM1. Further, we find that oleate deficiency is a host vulnerability that concomitantly activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) KGB-1 nutrient sensing pathway, an adaptive response that promotes expression of TIR-1/SARM1 on lysosome-related organelles and is required for survival during infection. These data establish a mechanistic connection between fatty acid nutrition and innate immune regulation, and reveal that specific changes in host metabolism are surveilled to identify pathogen attack.

papers.title: A mammalian fibroblast zoo reveals barriers to cross-species virus replication and differential regulation of antiviral immunity
papers.abstract: Virus zoonosis represents a continual threat to humans. Viruses emerge in humans directly or indirectly through interactions with mammals. However, our understanding of virus-host susceptibility across the diversity of mammals is limited and experimental model systems are restricted to a very small set of model organisms. Mammals are highly diverse and different habitats, lifestyles, diets, and exposures to different pathogens have driven substantial genetic diversity. We generated a library of primary fibroblasts across 86 mammalian species and used these cells to build an atlas of virus-host susceptibility across a panel of arboviruses that infect diverse mammals including humans. Perturbing the innate immune system revealed some virus-host pairs where restriction is controlled by the immune system and others where there is an incompatibility with host factors. Transcriptomic profiling of the library in response to virus sensing mimicked by poly(I:C) or antiviral signaling with type I interferon reveals a core set of conserved genes that respond as well as substantial species- and order-specific responses. Together these data provide a comparative atlas of innate immune responses across mammals and offer a window into how these systems have evolved across animals.
